'''Helios Murialdo''' ([[né]] Helios Murialdo Laport; born December 5, 1941) is a Chilean-Canadian molecular biologist,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cardiacehealth.academia.edu/HeliosMurialdo|title = Helios Murialdo &#124; University Health Network / University of Toronto - Academia.edu}}</ref> fiction writer, and ecologist. His research in the field of the assembly and structure of [[Bacteriophage|bacterial viruses]] contributed to the development of the first system for the [[cloning]] of human genes. He has published six novels and is a member of a group of conservationists that established a Natural Reserve in the central part of the Chilean [[Biodiversity hotspot|Biodiversity Hotspot]].<ref>Biodiversity hotspots. Conservation International. http://www.cnrs.fr/inee/recherche/fichiers/Biodiversite_hotspots.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170215065849/http://www.cnrs.fr/inee/recherche/fichiers/Biodiversite_hotspots.pdf |date=2017-02-15 }}</ref>
Son of an Italian immigrant father and a Chilean mother of French descent, he has a brother and a sister. He is a member of the board of directors of the non-profit Fundación Ciencia & Vida,<ref>Fundación Ciencia & Vida: http://www.cienciavida.org</ref> a scientific and technological institution with headquarters in [[Santiago|Santiago, Chile]]. He is president of the NGO Corporación Altos de Cantillana (Altos de Cantillana Corporation), which manages the 26,000 acres of the Altos de Cantillana Natural Reserve<ref>Corporación Altos de Cantillana: http://portal.mma.gob.cl/seremi-de-la-rm-visita-santuario-horcon-de-piedra-para-revisar-medidas-de-proteccion-ambiental-para-el-sector/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180306202612/http://portal.mma.gob.cl/seremi-de-la-rm-visita-santuario-horcon-de-piedra-para-revisar-medidas-de-proteccion-ambiental-para-el-sector/ |date=2018-03-06 }}</ref> in the coastal mountains of [[central Chile]]. He makes his home in this Natural Reserve, and spends the rest of the year in [[Toronto|Toronto, Canada]]. He is co-author of “The International Boundary in the Southern Patagonian Ice Field” alongside Juan Ignacio Ipinza and Cedomir Marangunic Damanovic.

==Biography==
Helios Murialdo obtained his MSc at the Faculty of Chemistry, [[University of Chile]], in 1965. He became an assistant professor in the Department of Biology, Faculty of Sciences, University of Chile and a lecturer in biochemistry in the Faculty of Agronomical Sciences, at the [[Catholic University of Chile]], in Santiago. He obtained his PhD in [[molecular biology]] at the Department of Medical Biophysics, [[University of Toronto]], Canada, in 1971, under the supervision of Dr. [[Louis Siminovitch]]. On his return to Chile he was appointed an associate professor in the Faculty of Sciences, University of Chile. From 1973 to 1998 he taught and carried out research in the Department of Molecular Genetics at the University of Toronto,<ref>Department of Molecular Genetics at the University of Toronto http://www.moleculargenetics.utoronto.ca/</ref> becoming a full professor in 1984. In that year, while teaching a theoretical and laboratory course at the Cuban Center for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology,<ref>Center for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, Havana, Cuba: http://biomed.cigb.edu.cu/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180404073816/http://biomed.cigb.edu.cu/ |date=2018-04-04 }}</ref> he introduced the technique of [[DNA cloning]] in [[Cuba]], which led to the establishment of the first sugar cane [[gene library]]. He returned to Chile in 1998 and joined Fundación Ciencia & Vida as a research scientist. He retired from active scientific research to write fiction in 2006. During his years as an academic, as a hobby he built cellos admired for their high quality and beautiful sound. He has two daughters from his first marriage to Evelyn Murialdo (née Loewe), former Director of Tenant and Community Services at [[Toronto Community Housing|Toronto Community Housing Corporation]]. He is now married to the artist Olga Beskoff.

==Research==

At the Department of Molecular Genetics at the University of Toronto, his research advanced the understanding of the [[morphogenesis]] and structure of bacterial viruses ([[bacteriophages]]).<ref>{{cite journal | pmid = 14569303 | doi=10.1139/o03-059 | volume=81 | title=The product of the bacteriophage lambda W gene: purification and properties | journal=Biochem Cell Biol | pages=307–15 | last1 = Murialdo | first1 = H | last2 = Xing | first2 = X | last3 = Tzamtzis | first3 = D | last4 = Haddad | first4 = A | last5 = Gold | first5 = M | issue=4 | year=2003}}</ref> This led to the development of the procedure that later allowed the cloning of human genes. His laboratory was the first to synthesize a complex bacterial virus from its protein components in vitro.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/0042-6822(77)90099-x | pmid=860404 | volume=78 | title=Studies on an in Vitro System for the Packaging and Maturation of Phage Lambda DNA | journal=Virology | pages=277–290 | last1 = Becker | first1 = A | last2 = Murialdo | first2 = H | last3 = Gold | first3 = M (1977) | issue=1 | year=1977}}</ref> His work showed that a specialized structure (the connector or portal) initiates the [[polymerization]] of the [[Icosahedral|icosahedral structure]] of bacterial viruses and provided the first solid evidence that the synthesis of viruses is similar to a [[Crystallization|crystallization process]] or a [[phase transition]]. His laboratory discovered the first [[overlapping gene]]s in bacterial viruses, the stimulation of a set of bacterial proteins synthesis upon virus infection, and showed directly, by [[Electron microscope|electron microscopy]], that a bacterial protein (IHF) bends DNA. He also worked on the factors that control [[immunoglobulin]] [[gene expression]], the structure of the genes and their rearrangement during [[B cell|B-cell]] differentiation. These experiments led to the discovery of the [[mutation]]al potential of [[retrovirus]] sequences in the mouse genome.<ref>Helios Murialdo's scientific contributions: https://www.researchgate.net/scientific-contributions/54818112_Helios_Murialdo
</ref> Looking back on his life's work, he surmises that his scientific papers will become obsolete and his novels outdated, but that his cellos will improve with time. Just as the best cellos today are those made by the Italian masters [[Guarneri]] and [[Antonio Stradivari|Stradivari]] in the 17th and 18th centuries, he hopes his cellos will continue to make music for the next three hundred years or more.
